newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France, Germany fail to seal EMU pact deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France, Germany fail to seal EMU pact deal.

text.p: France and Germany failed on Friday to bury their differences on a single currency, leaving Europe facing an uphill task to strike a deal on an EU stability pact in time for a summit in Amsterdam next week.
France's Socialist prime minister Lionel Jospin said the new government was committed to a single currency but wanted a fundamentally new approach to monetary union.
Its demands for a focus on growth and jobs must be given the same importance as the stability pact limiting budget deficits after the launch of a single currency.

He was speaking at a news conference here after a meeting between French and German leaders and ministers failed to end a dispute on the pact, agreed in Dublin last year and due for approval in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.

"Those who say we have a huge problem are wrong. Those who say we have no problem are wrong. We have a problem and we are going to solve it," French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told reporters.

He said it took time to work out a deal. France's new government, swept to power in an upset parliamentary election victory on June 1, raised its objections to the pact at an international meeting for the first time on Monday.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the summit talks had taken "a step to success, but we have to do more".
He said there would be intensive talks among European officials this weekend to try to strike a deal in time for a meeting of EU finance ministers on the eve of the summit.
But he acknowledged there was no guarantee. "We will have an answer maybe Sunday, maybe Monday, maybe next week," he said.
Economists said that while not ruling out an agreement in Amsterdam, signs so far were not very promising.
"It's not impossible, but it is far from being a done deal," Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said. "I also had the impression Jospin was not going to bend."

"There was nothing in anything that Strauss-Kahn or Jospin said that suggests that they are going to soften their position. They are sticking to their guns," Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais, said.
Both France and Germany were keen, however, to talk down any suggestion of a rift between Paris and Bonn, whose alliance is seen as crucial to pushing monetary union through in 1999.
"We observed that our views are very largely similar and wherever this is not the case a solution can easily be found," French President Jacques Chirac said.
"There's one point on which we all agree, and that's that we need to do everything, including making sacrifices, so that we can launch this single currency together in the agreed timetable," he said.

But a French source said Chirac, forced by his centre-right coalition's defeat to share power with a left-wing government, told German Chancellor Helmut Kohl the French election campaign had raised expectations which could make it harder to meet Maastricht treaty criteria on a single currency.

"The president presented the new situation in France, where things were said in the campaign and expectations were created that may be an additional complicating factor in achieving the criteria," the source said.
